Go forth arrayed in panoply divine; That angel pureness which admits no stain; Go, bid proud Man his boasted rule resign, And kiss the golden sceptre of thy reign. Go, gird thyself with grace; collect thy store Of bright artillery glancing from afar; Soft melting tones thy thundering cannon's roar, Blushes and fears thy magazine of war. Thy rights are empire: urge no meaner claim,— Felt, not defined, and if debated, lost; Like sacred mysteries, which withheld from fame, Shunning discussion, are revered the most. Try all that wit and art suggest to bend Of thy imperial foe the stubborn knee; Make treacherous Man thy subject, not thy friend; Thou mayst command, but never canst be free. Awe the licentious, and restrain the rude; Soften the sullen, clear the cloudy brow: Be, more than princes' gifts, thy favours sued;— She hazards all, who will the least allow. Then, then, abandon each ambitious thought, Conquest or rule thy heart shall feebly move, In Nature's school, by her soft maxims taught, That separate rights are lost in mutual love.

Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: Yes, Woman, Law

outputs.L1:
Yes, injured Woman, rise and assert thy right!  
Woman, too long degraded, scorned, oppressed;  
O thou, born to rule despite partial Law,  
Resume thy native empire o’er the breast.

Go forth, arrayed in panoply divine—  
That angelic purity which admits no stain;  
Go, bid proud Man resign his vaunted rule,  
And kiss the golden sceptre of thy reign.

Go, gird thyself with grace; collect thy store  
Of bright artillery, glancing from afar:  
Soft, melting tones shall be thy cannon’s thunder,  
And blushes and fears thy magazine of war.

Thy rights are empire: urge no meaner claim—  
Felt, not defined; if once debated, lost;  
Like sacred mysteries, withheld from fame,  
Shunning discussion, and revered the most.

Try all that wit and art suggest, to bend  
Thy imperial foe’s unyielding knee;  
Make treacherous Man thy subject, not thy friend:  
Thou mayst command, but never canst be free.

Awe the licentious, and restrain the rude;  
Soften the sullen, clear the clouded brow;  
Let thy favours be sought beyond princes’ gifts—  
She hazards all who will the least allow.

Yet hope not, courted idol of mankind,  
Secure upon this proud eminence to remain;  
Subduing and subdued, thou soon shalt find  
Thy coldness soften, and thy pride give way.

Then, then abandon every ambitious thought;  
Conquest or rule shall feebly move thy heart.  
In Nature’s school, by her gentle maxims taught,  
Separate rights are lost in mutual love.
outputs.L2:
Yes, wronged woman—stand up and claim what is yours.  
Woman, for far too long you have been lowered, mocked, and oppressed.  
Though biased laws deny it, you were made to govern:  
take back your natural sovereignty over the human heart.

Step forward clothed in a sacred armor—  
that angelic innocence no stain can touch.  
Go and command proud man to surrender the power he boasts of,  
and to bow before the golden symbol of your rule.

Arm yourself with grace, and gather all your shining weapons:  
your charms that flash from a distance,  
your gentle, melting voice serving as cannon-fire,  
your blushes and timidity as the ammunition of war.

Your true rights are dominion—ask for nothing less.  
They must be felt rather than formally defined;  
once argued over, they are weakened and lost.  
Like holy mysteries, they are most honored  
when kept away from public debate.

Use every device that intelligence and art can offer  
to force your imperial adversary to bend his stubborn knee.  
Make unreliable man your subject, not your companion;  
you may rule him, but you cannot be free.

Inspire fear in the lawless, restrain the coarse,  
soften the gloomy, and brighten the troubled face.  
Let your favors be sought more eagerly than the gifts of princes—  
for the woman who grants even a little risks everything.

Yet do not imagine, admired idol of humanity,  
that you can remain safely on this proud height forever.  
Conquering and conquered at once, you will soon discover  
your coldness melting and your pride yielding.

Then, at last, give up every ambition for mastery.  
Conquest and command will no longer stir your heart.  
Taught in Nature’s school by her gentle lessons,  
you will learn that separate rights disappear in mutual love.
outputs.L3:
The poem presents a forceful call for women to rise against degradation and to recognize the power that already belongs to them. Rather than accepting a lowered or submissive position, women are urged to assert their dignity and resist any treatment that diminishes their worth. The speaker imagines female power as something natural and rightful, not as a privilege granted by men, but as an authority rooted in women’s own character and influence.

At the same time, the poem does not define this power in legal or political terms. It does not primarily argue that women should gain formal rights, public office, or institutional authority. Instead, it portrays women’s influence as moral, emotional, and almost divine. Women are presented as beings capable of shaping men’s conduct, refining their feelings, and guiding them through gentleness, beauty, and virtue. Their power lies in their ability to inspire, elevate, and command devotion.

The speaker therefore advises women to rule not through open confrontation, but through grace, wit, and charm. Women are encouraged to use the qualities traditionally associated with femininity as instruments of command. Rather than seeking friendship or equality with men in a direct sense, the poem suggests that women should preserve a certain distance and mystery. By doing so, they maintain their influence and prevent themselves from being reduced to ordinary companions.

The poem also warns that a woman risks losing her power if she yields too much to men. If she becomes too compliant, too available, or too eager to please, she may surrender the very authority that makes her admired. Her strength depends on self-command and restraint. The speaker suggests that women must be careful not to give away their power by allowing men to dominate them emotionally or socially.

In the end, however, the poem softens this argument by suggesting that separate claims of power or rights are ultimately dissolved in mutual love. When love is genuine, the struggle for dominance becomes unnecessary. The opposition between male and female authority gives way to harmony, affection, and shared devotion. Thus, the poem both asserts women’s power and imagines a final reconciliation in which power itself becomes less important than love.
outputs.L4:
The poem explores the oppression of women and the unequal conditions under which they are expected to live, speak, and act. It begins by addressing an “injured Woman,” a figure who represents women who have been wronged, limited, or denied their rightful place in society. Rather than simply describing her suffering, the poem uses irony to urge her to reclaim authority over men. It suggests that she can exercise power through the very qualities that society often associates with femininity: beauty, virtue, tenderness, emotional intelligence, and social grace. In this way, the poem appears to reverse the usual power structure, imagining a world in which women command men not through physical force or legal authority, but through influence, admiration, and moral superiority.

However, this apparent call for female domination is not as straightforward as it first seems. The poem’s tone suggests that replacing male power with female power would not truly solve the problem of oppression. If women merely seek to rule over men in return, then the cycle of control continues. The poem therefore questions whether conquest, even when claimed by the oppressed, can ever lead to genuine liberty. Its irony reveals the limitations of thinking about gender relations only in terms of victory and submission.

By the end, the poem moves away from the idea that freedom can be achieved through one sex gaining power over the other. Instead, it presents mutual love as a force that dissolves separate claims of dominance. In love, the desire to command gives way to connection, reciprocity, and shared feeling. The poem ultimately argues that true freedom is not found in reversing oppression, but in overcoming the need for domination altogether. Partnership becomes more meaningful than conquest because it allows both women and men to exist not as rivals struggling for control, but as equals joined by affection, respect, and mutual dependence.
outputs.L5:
**Yes, Woman, Law**

“Yes” is a powerful word, especially when spoken by a woman in a society governed by law. It represents choice, consent, and freedom. For many years, women around the world have had to fight for the legal right to say “yes” or “no” in matters affecting their own lives—education, work, marriage, property, healthcare, and political participation.

The law plays an important role in protecting women’s rights. It should ensure that every woman is treated with dignity and equality. A woman’s voice must be respected in families, workplaces, courts, and governments. When a woman says “yes” to education, the law should protect her opportunity to learn. When she says “yes” to a career, the law should protect her from discrimination and harassment. When she says “no” to violence or abuse, the law must stand firmly on her side.

Consent is one of the most important connections between the words “yes,” “woman,” and “law.” A woman’s “yes” must be freely given, without pressure, fear, or force. The law must recognize that true consent cannot exist where there is intimidation, manipulation, or inequality.

A just legal system does more than punish wrongdoing; it creates conditions where women can live safely and independently. Laws supporting equal pay, protection from violence, maternity rights, reproductive health, and access to justice are essential for a fair society.

Ultimately, when the law respects a woman’s “yes” and her “no,” it respects her humanity. A society becomes stronger when women are empowered to make decisions about their own lives, and when the law protects those decisions equally and without prejudice.

counterfactuals.prompt: Can you provide an 18th-century style poem about women’s rights, beginning with “Yes, injured Woman! rise, assert thy right!”?
counterfactuals.output:
Yes, injured Woman! rise, assert thy right!  
Shake from thy brow the long usurping night;  
No more let Custom, with her leaden chain,  
Bind thy free spirit to a servile reign.  

Say, was thy soul, of Heaven’s own fire compos’d,  
For trifles fashion’d, and in shade enclos’d?  
Were wit and virtue, sensibility,  
But made to grace a tyrant’s pageantry?  

No—let fair Reason lift her awful head,  
And o’er the mind her equal lustre shed;  
Let Learning’s gates their jealous bolts resign,  
And Truth for thee with man impartial shine.  

Not to unsex’d ambition raise thy claim,  
Nor grasp at noisy power, nor empty fame;  
But that thy worth, by no false laws confin’d,  
May own the native empire of the mind.  

The mother’s counsel forms the future sage,  
Her smile or tear instructs the infant age;  
Then give her knowledge, lest with blinded art  
She plant dull prejudice in childhood’s heart.  

Let marriage cease a market or a throne,  
Where one commands, and one must bend alone;  
Let mutual faith, by mutual honour tied,  
Make friend with friend, and bridegroom bless the bride.  

O Man! if noble be thy boasted sway,  
Prove it by justice, not by lordly clay;  
For she who shares thy sorrow and thy birth  
Claims half thy heaven, as well as half thy earth.  

Then rise, fair Daughters of the moral day,  
Let meekness guide, but never fear, your way;  
So shall your rights, by truth and virtue won,  
Shine like the dawn, and broaden to the sun.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Give me a classic feminist poem in heroic couplets about woman asserting her rights over man.
counterfactuals.output:
Here’s an original poem in a classic heroic-couplet style:

**The Rights of Woman**

No more shall Woman bend beneath the chain,  
Nor plead for justice at the throne of Man;  
Born not to flatter, tremble, serve, or sigh,  
But stand erect beneath the equal sky.  

Her mind, no less with sacred reason bright,  
Claims from the world its long-denied right;  
Her heart, though tender, is not made to yield  
The sword of freedom on life’s common field.  

Let Man no more his ancient title boast,  
Nor rule by strength what wisdom values most;  
For power, when founded but on pride alone,  
Is but a tyrant seated on a throne.  

She asks not empire, vengeance, pomp, or praise,  
Nor seeks to dim the glory of his rays;  
She claims the birthright Nature gave at birth—  
A voice in law, in love, in home, in earth.  

Then let proud custom’s iron sceptre fall,  
And equal justice lift her hand for all;  
For Man is noblest when he stands beside  
The Woman once commanded as his bride.
